title: Log Lane Village Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Log Lane Village wells have a 100-ft median depth, 15 gpm median reported yield, and estimated finished costs of $9,500-$17,500.
h1: Wells and Water in Log Lane Village, Colorado
intro_html:
Well records around Log Lane Village show a shallow plains setting, with a median drilled depth of 100 feet. The middle half runs from 68 to 126 feet, and reported yields are generally strong, although only a portion of permitted wells includes a pump-yield measurement.

This area is different from Colorado’s deeper Denver Basin communities. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, while other records identify Quaternary Alluvium or Alluvial water. Before buying land near Morgan Heights, Trail Side, Fort Morgan, Blue Sky, or Saddle Ridge, use nearby well records as a starting point, then confirm water rights, well condition, septic suitability, and the cost of a new installation.

sections.heading: Log Lane Village well depth and local ground conditions
sections.html:
The typical well near Log Lane Village is not especially deep. The median reported total depth is 100 feet, and the middle half of wells falls between 68 and 126 feet. About 48% are under 100 feet, while 51% are between 100 and 300 feet. Only 1% reaches 300 to 600 feet, and no wells in this dataset are recorded at 600 feet or deeper.

The deepest record is 540 feet, so a shallow bid should not be treated as a guarantee. Local drilling crosses alluvium and plains sedimentary material, with many permits naming an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. A driller should review nearby completions, casing and grout requirements, and the specific lot before setting a target depth.

sections.heading: Reported well yield near Fort Morgan and Morgan Heights
sections.html:
Among the wells that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 220.0 gallons per minute, and 94% of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. The records show 6% producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, with none reported below 5 gallons per minute.

That is encouraging for a buyer, but the yield sample is limited: 283 wells report a pump yield out of 1,944 permits. A reported yield is also not the same as guaranteed household supply. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information, storage capacity, and any production limits before relying on the number for a home, livestock, or irrigation plan.

sections.heading: What the Log Lane Village water levels show
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 35 feet below the surface. The middle half lies between 16 and 50 feet. That shallow water level can reduce pumping lift, but it also makes proper casing, grout, and wellhead protection important. A shallow water table is more exposed to local surface conditions than a deep, isolated water source.

The decade series does not show a simple steadily dropping pattern. The median was 30 feet below surface in the 1950s, 22 feet in the 2010s, and 38 feet in the 2020s. These measurements come from different wells and dates, so they are not a substitute for a site-specific water-level check. Only 71 records report a static water level.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers serving this part of Morgan County
sections.html:
Permit records show a long drilling history around Log Lane Village. The database contains 1,944 permitted wells, with 1,449 recorded as constructed. Permits were issued in every listed decade from the 1950s through the 2020s, and the newest permit year is 2025. The use mix is mainly domestic or household at 53%, followed by irrigation at 18% and stock at 15%.

The most frequently named driller in these records is Canfield Drilling Company, also shown as Canfield, Harold E, with 334 records. Canfield, Leslie George appears on 192, and Authorized (Pe, Pg) appears on 147. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation or proof that a contractor is currently available.

sections.heading: What a new well costs in Log Lane Village
sections.html:
For the local alluvium and plains sedimentary ground, the drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the median depth of 100 feet, the drilled hole works out to roughly $3,500 to $5,500. That is only the drilling portion, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,500 to $17,500 at the median depth. A lot requiring a deeper hole, difficult access, longer trenching, or unusual casing and grout work can fall outside that range. Get a written bid that separates drilling, casing, pump equipment, electrical, trenching, testing, and permitting so competing proposals can be compared.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Trail Side or Weldona
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main warning sign in the reported records, but dry holes and variable production remain possible because local results differ by location and the yield sample is limited. A buyer should inspect the actual well report, pump test, static level, construction details, and water-quality results rather than relying only on the area median.

Environmental review also matters. The mapped area has 23 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. No historic mine features are mapped there. Test existing water for the risks relevant to the property, and keep septic setbacks, replacement-field space, drainage, access for drilling, and building placement in the site plan. An exempt household-use well may still be subject to permit conditions, and over-appropriated basins may require an augmentation plan.

sections.heading: A practical plan for buying or building on a Log Lane Village lot
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit number and construction report for any existing well. Compare that well with nearby records in Log Lane Village, Morgan Heights, Fort Morgan, Blue Sky, Saddle Ridge, and Weldona. The local median depth and yield are useful for budgeting, but they do not establish the capacity or legal use of one particular well.

For vacant land, have a licensed driller review access, likely depth, casing and grout, pump placement, and the proposed septic area before closing. Confirm the permitted use: domestic, stock, irrigation, or monitoring records are not interchangeable. For a home, budget the complete system rather than drilling alone, arrange water testing, and confirm whether the planned household use fits the permit. Colorado’s exempt-well pumping limit is 35 gpm, but permit terms and basin administration still control what can legally be done.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Log Lane Village?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Log Lane Village is 100 feet. The middle half of records runs from 68 to 126 feet. About 48% are under 100 feet, while 51% fall between 100 and 300 feet. The deepest record is 540 feet, so a driller should review nearby completions before pricing a specific lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Log Lane Village?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $35 to $55 per foot. At the 100-foot median depth, drilling alone is estimated at $3,500 to $5,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,500 to $17,500. Deeper drilling, difficult access, or additional construction requirements can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near Log Lane Village?
faq.a: Reported wells have a median pump yield of 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 220.0 gallons per minute, and 94% of reported wells exceed 15 gallons per minute. However, only 283 wells report a yield, so the property’s own pump test and well report matter more than the area statistic.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Log Lane Village?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that water is safe to drink. There are 23 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the actual well water before occupancy, review the wellhead and septic layout, and use treatment recommended for the laboratory results.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Log Lane Village?
faq.a: The reported decade medians do not show a simple steady decline. Static water levels were 30 feet below surface in the 1950s, 22 feet in the 2010s, and 38 feet in the 2020s. Only 71 wells report static water levels, and the measurements come from different wells, so they cannot prove a trend for one property.
